summary: Sacramento County sprawls across nearly a thousand square miles of Central Valley floor where the American and Sacramento Rivers converge — a fact that gives the region something few inland California counties can claim: a genuine riverfront identity, with over 30 miles of paved parkway tracing the American River from downtown eastward toward the Sierra foothills. That river corridor is the connective tissue an otherwise car-dependent county badly needs, because beyond the urban core and a handful of gridded older neighborhoods, much of the landscape is subdivisions separated by wide arterials and freeway interchanges linking places like Elk Grove, Citrus Heights, and Rancho Cordova. The job picture is anchored by state government — California's capital employs tens of thousands of public-sector workers — supplemented by two major health systems (UC Davis Medical Center and Sutter Health) and a growing logistics sector fed by proximity to I-5 and rail lines. At a median home price around $499,000 against $88,700 in household income, the price-to-income ratio lands near 5.6 — steep, but roughly half the squeeze of coastal Bay Area counties, which partly explains the county's steady population growth. Summers are genuinely hot, with average highs well into the 90s from June through September and over nine hours of daily sunshine year-round, while winters are mild and gray enough to feel like a different place entirely. Motor vehicle theft running at roughly 670 per 100,000 is one of the highest rates in the state, a persistent infrastructure and policy challenge. Sacramento County is, at its core, an affordable-by-California-standards government and healthcare hub that offers river access and Sierra proximity in exchange for Central Valley heat and the sprawl patterns that come with rapid inland growth.
